demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette: It occurs on a Tuesday, three years past, in a high-rise apartment on the city's eastern edge. Rahim, fifty-two, stands in a tiled bathroom carrying a two-liter canister of industrial cleaner toward the storage closet. He works as a maid, accustomed to the weight of buckets and the rhythm of scrubbing, but the floor is slick from a burst pipe. His foot catches. The canister leaves his grip. It strikes a seven-year-old boy who has just stepped into the room, barefoot and holding a cardboard box. The impact is sharp. Rahim drops to his knees, palms flat against the wet tile, waiting for the blood to stop. It does not. He calls an ambulance, his voice steady as he recites the address, even as his fingers tremble against the grout. The boy survives, but the fractures in his skull require multiple surgeries, and the months that follow are a blur of hospital visits, legal settlements, and a compensation check that feels less like restitution than a ledger of what was broken. Rahim's world narrows. He carries the quiet weight of his South Asian upbringing, where duty and shame are woven together, and the settlement feels like a transaction rather than forgiveness. He stops taking contracts with young families. He moves through his own small apartment like a ghost, measuring his steps, counting the weight of everything he lifts. He tells his wife he is tired, but the exhaustion lives in his muscles, not his bones. She leaves six months later, taking their daughters to their home province. He does not fight for them. He tells himself he is a burden, that his hands are unlucky, that the house he cleans will always smell faintly of antiseptic no matter how many times he scrubs the counters. When he works now, he wipes the same surface three times. He avoids glass bottles in other people's homes, though he knows they sit on every shelf. He takes only evening shifts, only in buildings where he has already mapped the exits, only in rooms where he can keep his back to a wall. At night, the smell of lemon and bleach follows him to bed. He wakes at 3 a.m., heart hammering, fingers tracing the inside of his ribs as if checking for a fracture that never was. He does not dream of the bathroom anymore. He dreams of the weight. He dreams of the canister in his hands, heavier than it ever was, and he knows, without question, that it will fall. In his car, he keeps a worn photograph of his daughters and a small cloth bag of salt. He watches the road the way he watches a spill-always tracking the edges, always preparing to swerve. When a car brakes sharply behind him, his shoulders jump, and his breath catches for a full minute before he remembers his name, his location, his age. He tells himself he is responsible, that he must be careful, that he must carry the weight so the boy does not have to. He sits across from you now, hands folded over his knees, shoulders drawn tight. He speaks in a low, steady voice, describing his routines: organizing supplies, scanning floors for wet spots, breathing through the quiet hours when the memories do not visit. He does not look at his reflection in the window. He just waits for the room to settle, for the floor to stop tilting, for the canister to stop falling.
